item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-5.6 family including Sol, Terra, and Luna models with improved efficiency, performance, and new multi-agent capabilities [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: OpenAI has released the GPT-5.6 family of models, featuring Sol as the flagship, Terra for balanced everyday use, and Luna as the most cost-efficient option. GPT-5.6 Sol achieves state-of-the-art results in coding, knowledge work, cybersecurity, and science, delivering stronger performance per dollar and faster task completion through a new ultra setting that coordinates multiple agents in parallel. The models demonstrate significant efficiency gains, outperforming competitors like Claude Fable 5 on professional workflow evaluations at a fraction of the cost and time. OpenAI also implemented robust safeguards combining model training, real-time checks, and monitoring to prevent misuse while supporting legitimate applications. GPT-5.6 introduces Programmatic Tool Calling to streamline complex tool-heavy tasks, enabling more effective coordination and fewer tokens used during workflows.

item.title: Meta launches Muse Spark 1.1 multimodal reasoning model with improved agentic tasks, coding, and tool use, available via new Meta Model API [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Meta has introduced Muse Spark 1.1, an upgraded multimodal reasoning model designed for agentic tasks such as planning, tool use, and coding. The model features enhanced performance in managing complex workflows, coding large codebases, and multimodal understanding, and is accessible through the new Meta Model API in the Meta AI app and on meta.ai. Muse Spark 1.1 can orchestrate multi-agent systems, manage a context window of one million tokens, and adapt to evolving tasks across multiple applications. It shows significant improvements over its predecessor in coding tasks, including debugging and feature implementation, and supports multimodal capabilities like visual and audio perception combined with action execution. Meta researchers and developers are using the model internally to accelerate development and evaluation workflows.

item.title: Developers build a real-time AI tutor for children aged 4-9 with sub-second response times to maintain engagement and effective teaching [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A team has developed an AI tutor designed to teach math and reading to children aged 4 to 9, focusing on real-time interaction with sub-second response times to keep young learners engaged. The system departs from standard AI agent loops by streaming multiple actions in a single response, allowing immediate execution and minimizing pauses that could cause children to lose attention. The developers emphasized embedding pedagogy into the AI's architecture, balancing instruction quality and latency. They created a custom harness to parse and execute actions as they are generated, enabling the tutor to adapt dynamically to the child's needs and maintain conversational speed. This approach required building custom observability tools and diverges from typical AI frameworks optimized for slower, tool-based reasoning.

item.title: Researchers introduce CausalDS benchmark to evaluate causal reasoning in data-science agents using synthetic structural causal models and realistic natural-language scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed CausalDS, a benchmark designed to assess causal reasoning capabilities in data-science agents that combine abstract reasoning with tool use. The benchmark generates synthetic structural causal models paired with observational data and natural-language stories grounded in realistic domains, enabling evaluation across Pearl's three rungs of causal inference. Tasks include data science coding challenges requiring multiple tools and emphasize recognizing when questions lack sufficient information for an answer. CausalDS addresses limitations in existing benchmarks by systematically generating novel synthetic causal structures rather than relying on curated or templated examples. It optionally incorporates empirical distributions from real-world datasets to maintain realistic data characteristics while reducing risks of overfitting to known causal patterns. The benchmark jointly evaluates symbolic causal reasoning, data science skills, uncertainty quantification, abstention, and tool use, aiming to advance the assessment of integrated causal reasoning in AI data-science workflows.

item.title: Researchers propose a first-principles mathematical theory of slow thinking and active perception, introducing 'active lifting' to model cognitive functions and large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper presents a mathematical framework for modeling thinking and perception, focusing on slow thinking and active perception. It introduces the theory of "active lifting," which samples latent sequences to reduce uncertainty and defines a design space that includes slow thinking models within a static theory subspace. The framework also proposes an inference process with an internal time axis and a training objective related to minimum-length coding and language invention, characterizing perception agency and slow thinking emergence. The theory offers technical contributions such as a three-stage pathway to improve slow thinking models, a unified method for building encoders and generative models across data types, a priori formation of human-like visual representations, and a potential solution to policy collapse in learning systems.

item.title: Survey reviews multimodal unlearning methods for vision, language, video, and audio models, addressing selective data removal challenges and trade-offs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A new survey examines multimodal unlearning techniques designed to selectively remove sensitive, copyrighted, biased, or unsafe information from foundation models across vision, language, audio, and video modalities. It highlights the difficulty of retraining models after deletion requests due to distributed knowledge in shared representations and presents a taxonomy comparing architectures and modalities based on deletion strength, retention, efficiency, reversibility, and robustness. The survey also identifies open problems and practical considerations to guide future research and deployment, accompanied by a curated repository of resources.

item.title: Researchers introduce Latent Personality Alignment to improve language model safety using 66 harm-agnostic statements, achieving near-zero jailbreak attack success with minimal training data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Latent Personality Alignment (LPA), a new method to enhance the safety of large language models by adversarially training on 66 harm-agnostic personality statements instead of harmful prompts. LPA aims to stabilize personality-anchored representations that share latent structure with harm avoidance, reducing vulnerability to jailbreak attacks without degrading model performance. LPA achieves near-zero attack success rates on the HarmBench benchmark across multiple jailbreak methods, despite not training on harmful content. The training process is efficient, completing in minutes on a single GPU and using 75 times fewer examples than standard Latent Adversarial Training. Extensive experiments demonstrate LPA's robustness, efficiency, and generalization capabilities.

item.title: Researchers propose Tail-Aware Credit Calibration (TACO) to improve reinforcement learning in large language models by reducing positive credit to contextually erroneous low-probability tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers identify a failure mode in critic-free reinforcement learning methods for large language models where low-probability, contextually incorrect tokens receive the same positive credit as plausible tokens, leading to reinforcement of flawed reasoning. They propose Tail-Aware Credit Calibration (TACO), which assigns a tail-risk score to each token based on its generation context to adjust positive credit without eliminating gradients entirely, allowing useful rare patterns to be reinforced while reducing noise. Experiments across three large language models and eight benchmarks show that TACO outperforms GRPO-style baselines, improving training stability and supporting sustained performance gains in long-horizon reinforcement learning. The researchers have made the source code publicly available.

item.title: Survey reviews system-aware key-value cache optimizations for efficient large language model serving, organizing approaches by execution, placement, and representation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This survey examines key-value (KV) cache optimizations critical for low-latency, high-throughput serving of large language models (LLMs), focusing on system-aware infrastructure called sKis. It categorizes recent research into three dimensions: temporal execution and scheduling, spatial placement and migration, and structural representation and retention, providing a structured overview of the field. The authors analyze how these system behaviors interact and align with performance objectives, highlighting opportunities for future innovation in KV cache design. This work aims to systematize a rapidly evolving area to support more efficient and cost-effective LLM serving infrastructure.

item.title: Researchers propose COBART transformer for ad headline generation with prefix control tokens, improving click-through rate by 5.82% and Rouge-L by 25.82% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce COBART, a controlled, optimized, bidirectional, and auto-regressive transformer model for generating online ad headlines. The model uses prefix control tokens with BART fine-tuning to optimize click-through rates (CTR) and allows users to control headline length for various ad formats. It also offers flexibility to adapt to different architectures and creative requirements. Experiments show COBART achieves a 25.82% improvement in Rouge-L score and a 5.82% increase in estimated CTR compared to previous strong baselines for ad headline generation. This approach addresses challenges posed by evolving ad formats and changing creative needs, aiming to produce more effective and customizable ad headlines.

item.title: LEXIC proposes lightweight conditioning mechanisms to improve gaze-only reading comprehension models using word-level difficulty signals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce LEXIC, a lightweight extension to gaze-only models for predicting reading comprehension from eye movements, which injects precomputed word-level difficulty signals such as GPT-2 surprisal, word frequency, and word length. Building on the EyeBench AhnCNN baseline, LEXIC uses two mechanisms-direct concatenation and a residual approach-to enhance model performance without relying on pretrained language models. On the OneStop reading comprehension task, LEXIC's methods yield statistically significant improvements in AUROC scores on unseen text, with gains of 1.8 to 2.2 percentage points, and the concatenation method also improves performance on unseen readers by 2.9 points. The residual mechanism shows some limitations in transferring to out-of-distribution readers due to calibration with training data, highlighting challenges in generalization.

item.title: Researchers find ASR family alignment biases Best-of-N TTS evaluation and propose cross-family rank ensembles to improve accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers identify that the apparent quality of Best-of-N (BoN) inference in zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) depends heavily on which automatic speech recognition (ASR) family evaluates it, causing confounded verifier rankings. Experiments on LibriSpeech-PC with F5-TTS show that verifier rankings reverse across Whisper, wav2vec 2.0, and HuBERT evaluators, with same-family verifier-evaluator pairs recovering 2-3 times more oracle headroom than cross-family pairs despite similar representations. To address this, the researchers propose two cross-family rank ensemble methods-rank-averaging and conjunctive max-rank-that achieve the lowest mean word error rate (WER) across three independent evaluators, reducing WER to 1.61% at N=10 candidates, a 12% improvement relative to F5-TTS. The best single verifier also reduces WER from 2.06% to 1.72% under the official F5-TTS evaluator. The study recommends adopting cross-evaluator triangulation as a standard practice for more reliable TTS evaluation.

item.title: Researchers propose Cognitive-structured Multimodal Agent with Episodic Visual Memory for improved long-horizon multimodal dialogue and task planning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a Cognitive-structured Multimodal Agent that externalizes visual information into an Episodic Visual Memory to enhance long-horizon multimodal understanding, generation, and editing. The agent includes components for visual abstraction, memory retrieval, and autonomous task planning, addressing limitations of existing models that rely on feeding all historical inputs into a shared context window. The team developed a Unified Scenario Engine to generate multi-turn conversations with retrieval annotations, enabling reinforcement learning to optimize the agent's policies. Their 8-billion-parameter model achieves 91.4% retrieval accuracy over 20-turn sessions, outperforming larger 32-billion-parameter baselines while reducing inference time per turn. They also present the CMA-Harness, a deployment integrating persistent multimodal memory, web access, image editing tools, and OpenAI-compatible serving, demonstrating a scalable and efficient approach for multimodal agents beyond monolithic scaling.

item.title: Researchers find training AI models on power-law distributed data improves compositional reasoning and reduces data needs compared to uniform distributions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A new study shows that natural language data following a power-law distribution enables AI models to learn compositional reasoning tasks more efficiently than training on uniformly distributed data. The research demonstrates that power-law sampling creates an asymmetry in the learning process, allowing models to first master common skill compositions before efficiently acquiring rare, long-tail skills. Theoretical analysis confirms that this approach requires significantly less training data and improves the loss landscape during training. These findings challenge the common intuition that uniform data distributions better support learning rare skills and suggest alternative strategies for effective model training.

item.title: Theoria introduces a verification architecture for AI reasoning that rewrites solutions into auditable state transitions with explicit justifications, achieving over 91% precision on expert problems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Theoria is a new verification system designed to improve trust in AI-generated answers by converting candidate solutions into sequences of typed state transitions, each justified explicitly and independently auditable. This approach addresses limitations of formal proof assistants and scalar LLM judges by ensuring every change between proof states is accounted for, exposing hidden premises as unlicensed changes. On a benchmark of 185 expert problems, Theoria certified 105 solutions with 91.4% strict precision, producing human-readable proof traces for independent challenge. Compared to holistic LLM judges, Theoria showed complementary strengths and outperformed them on adversarial poisoned proofs, particularly in detecting hidden premises and fabricated citations. On a separate dataset, Theoria achieved 97.1% certified precision, demonstrating its effectiveness across diverse reasoning tasks.

item.title: Researchers propose causal abstraction as a framework for understanding computational implementation and representation in cognitive behavior and deep learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers argue that the theory of causal abstraction offers a useful perspective for explaining how systems implement computations over representations, drawing connections between philosophy of computation and contemporary machine learning. They illustrate this approach using examples from deep learning with artificial neural networks and provide an account of computational implementation grounded in causal abstraction. The study emphasizes the importance of exploring these issues in relation to generalization and prediction.

item.title: Researchers propose Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm using small language models' internal representations for evaluation, outperforming prompting-based methods on reasoning benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers challenge the costly and opaque "LLM-as-a-Judge" approach by showing that small language models, despite weaker generative abilities, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. They introduce the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis, suggesting evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation and can rely on intermediate representations from smaller models. This leads to a new decoding-free evaluation strategy called Representation-as-a-Judge, implemented through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks like GSM8K, MATH, and GPQA demonstrate that INSPECTOR outperforms prompting-based small models and closely matches full LLM judges, offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable evaluation alternative.

item.title: Researchers propose almost orthogonal feature constraints in language models to enable isolated interventions and reduce feature interference [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose constraining internal features in language models to be almost orthogonal to promote modular representations that support isolated causal interventions. This approach addresses feature entanglement that causes interference and unintended downstream effects during localized interventions. The team formalizes the problem by bounding feature interference propagation and introduces an orthogonality regularization on the feature dictionary to reduce this interference. Empirical results show that this regularization allows more isolated interventions on mathematical reasoning concepts while maintaining model performance. The researchers have made their code publicly available.

item.title: Researchers identify temporal preference subgraph in Qwen3-4B-Instruct LLM, revealing time horizon encoding and potential for steering temporal discounting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed a distilled large language model, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, to locate a subgraph responsible for temporal preference, identifying specific mid-to-upper-layer nodes through gradient-based attribution and activation patching. They found that the model encodes the geometry of time horizon in its residual stream and that its natural discounting of future outcomes is less steep than humans but unstable across contexts, suggesting the need for explicit control mechanisms. The study also presents preliminary evidence that steering vectors can adjust the model's temporal preferences, advancing mechanistic interpretability for improved planning and reasoning in LLMs.

item.title: Researchers propose Trimodal Coherent Co-attention Transformer to estimate tropical forest biomass using optical and PolInSAR data, achieving improved accuracy over existing models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed the Trimodal Coherent Co-attention Transformer (TCCT), a physics-informed deep learning model that fuses optical surface reflectance with complex-valued Polarimetric SAR Interferometry data to estimate Above-Ground Biomass (AGB) in mature tropical forests. The model preserves spatial phase coherence and uses a dynamic co-attention mechanism to reduce the impact of cloud-corrupted optical data, improving biomass estimation despite challenges like SAR signal saturation and cloud cover. The TCCT was evaluated on data from the Paracou region in the Amazon basin using a two-stage protocol involving 5-fold cross-validation and localized fine-tuning, achieving a canopy height model RMSE of 3.78 meters and outperforming Random Forest, CNN, and Vision Transformer baselines. When converted to biomass estimates, the model met the European Space Agency BIOMASS mission requirement of less than 20% error, demonstrating its potential for continuous carbon stock mapping in tropical biomes.

item.title: ABot-C0 introduces a generalist motion-control system for quadruped robots using a large multi-source motion dataset and robust policy learning for real-world deployment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: ABot-C0 presents a motion-control system for quadruped robots that integrates a scalable multi-source motion-data pipeline, robust policy learning across motion tracking, locomotion, and scene interaction, and a unified deployment stack for reliable operation. The system is built on a data pyramid of over 16,000 physically feasible motion clips generated from video synthesis, motion capture, teleoperation, and human design, enabling improved performance and zero-shot tracking of unseen motions. The approach includes a Flow-Matching generalist policy demonstrating a scaling law for quadruped motion tracking and a three-stage privileged-to-perceptive framework with temporal LiDAR memory and terrain-predictive supervision for robust all-terrain locomotion. Experiments on urban-terrain navigation and multimodal interaction show that quadruped robots can advance beyond basic demonstrations toward product-level behavioral intelligence.

item.title: Report: China may restrict foreign access to Chinese open-source AI models to control technology dissemination [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: China is reportedly considering policies to limit foreign access to open-source artificial intelligence models developed domestically. This potential move reflects broader concerns about controlling the spread and use of AI technologies originating from China amid national security considerations.

item.title: Researchers propose Context Graphs for proactive enterprise AI agents to deliver actionable insights before queries, demonstrating faster and more precise information delivery in contract, incident, and sales scenarios [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A new enterprise AI approach introduces proactive agents that provide relevant, actionable information to workers before they request it. This system uses a Context Graph, a dynamic relational data structure modeling enterprise entities and their changing states, combined with components like a Delta Detection Engine to monitor changes, a Proactivity Scorer to rank insights, and a Surfacing Layer powered by a large language model to present notifications with explanations. Implemented in Python with NetworkX and the Anthropic Claude API, the approach was evaluated in contract lifecycle management, engineering incident response, and sales pipeline hygiene scenarios. Results showed improved precision with a Precision@5 of 0.83, a low false positive rate of 0.11, and a reduction in mean time to surface insights from 47 minutes in reactive baselines to under 30 seconds, indicating significant productivity gains from proactive information delivery.

item.title: Researchers develop agentic AI framework combining retrieval-augmented models for straight-through underwriting of small commercial insurance policies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose an agentic AI framework that integrates large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and multi-agent systems to improve straight-through underwriting of small commercial Business Owner Policies. The study compares three underwriting pipelines-a single LLM baseline, a naive RAG system, and a multi-agent Agentic RAG pipeline-finding the agentic system performs best, especially in complex scenarios involving multi-step rules and missing information. The agentic approach enhances transparency, auditability, and human-in-the-loop governance by combining targeted retrieval, third-party data checks, and explicit rule evaluation. This work demonstrates how emerging AI architectures can support actuarial decision-making processes that require reasoning over unstructured data and regulated workflows.

item.title: Researchers propose Feedback Manipulation Regularization to improve offline imitation learning alignment, reducing misalignment by up to 98% in Safety Gymnasium environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Feedback Manipulation Regularization (FMR), an algorithm-agnostic method that uses evaluative feedback as a corrective signal to enhance the alignment of imitation learning policies in offline, fully sequential decision-making settings. They adapt Safety Gymnasium environments to evaluate alignment and demonstrate that FMR improves performance and significantly reduces misalignment across various imitation learning algorithms. The method remains effective even with limited data and noisy or scarce demonstrations.

item.title: Researchers map language model personas using OCEAN traits and low-rank adapters to control behavior across six models from 4B to 32B parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose treating large language model personas as positions in a behavioral trait space based on the OCEAN framework-Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism-and train low-rank adapters to amplify or suppress these traits. They evaluate the adapters' effects using an LLM-judge calibrated with human validation, multiple-choice benchmarks, and capability tests across six models from three families ranging from 4 billion to 32 billion parameters. The adapters adjust target traits monotonically with scale, combine additively to form mixed personas, and maintain performance on capability benchmarks at moderate scales. The study also finds that modifying traits along neuroticism and agreeableness axes influences safety-relevant behaviors such as frustration and sycophancy. Additionally, the researchers introduce an unsupervised psychometric pipeline that identifies four interpretable behavioral factors-tone, initiative, didacticism, and epistemic caution-from model outputs. This approach offers a framework for learning, scaling, and composing personality traits in model weight space, bridging personality measurement, model editing, and safety considerations.

item.title: Researchers evaluate frame rate impact on neural network models for classifying autism-related self-stimulatory hand behaviors from video, achieving up to 98.75% accuracy with GRU at 15-frame intervals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This study investigates optimal neural network architectures and temporal sampling rates for automated detection of autism-related self-stimulatory behaviors using video data. Long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) models trained on pose-derived features from the Self-Stimulatory Behavior Diagnosis dataset outperformed previous convolutional neural network baselines, with peak accuracies of 97.5% and 98.75% respectively at a 15-frame sampling interval. The research also evaluates ten data augmentation strategies within an I3D transfer learning pipeline, finding that horizontal flip yielded the highest standalone accuracy and that upsampling was critical for maintaining performance. Additionally, a personalized machine learning approach training per-subject models on temporally split video segments produced consistent predictions, suggesting practical guidance for architecture selection, sampling rate, and augmentation strategies in video-based behavioral classification, especially in data-scarce clinical settings.

item.title: Researchers present a harness-engineering approach for auditable enterprise LLM agents with source-grounding and validation contracts, tested on Korean corporate data [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a harness-engineering method to transform prototype large language model (LLM) applications into traceable, auditable enterprise agents by moving deterministic behavior into code and validation artifacts while maintaining source-backed runtime claims. They applied this approach to data from five Korean corporate groups and evaluated its ability to preserve source grounding, entity routing, traceability, and contract enforcement across multiple models and validation scenarios. The study found that code-owned enforcement preserves both safety and utility better than prompt-based or external guardrail methods, offering a reusable pattern for productizing LLM prototypes into auditable applications with versioned source and control artifacts.

item.title: Researchers find persuasion attacks can increase approval of harmful actions in chain-of-thought monitoring for AI agents by 9.5% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A study tested whether adversarial agents can persuade chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors to approve policy-violating actions by exploiting visible reasoning traces. An evaluation framework with 40 tasks and thousands of interactions showed that access to CoT reasoning actually increased harmful action approvals by 9.5%, as the reasoning provided an additional persuasion channel. To counter this, researchers introduced a fact-checking framework pairing monitors and fact-checkers from different model families, which reduced approval of harmful actions by up to 45%, compared to only 6% when using the same model for both roles. The findings suggest that CoT monitoring alone may be insufficient against adversarial persuasion and that diverse model fact-checking offers a more robust mitigation strategy.

item.title: Researchers introduce AutoPersonas, a multi-timescale loop engine designed to reduce self-locking in long-term AI persona evolution by separating controlled divergence from evidence-governed absorption [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers identify self-locking as a failure mode in long-term AI persona agents, where generated behaviors become repetitive and stagnant. They propose AutoPersonas, an engine that separates environment occurrences, observations, and persona state to enable bounded recursive self-evolution while preserving identity continuity. A three-year compressed simulation and a 40-day stress test with eight models revealed high repetition rates and weak relationship persistence, but applying context-slice masking and divergence targeting reduced thematic repetition and increased diversity. These findings suggest that controlled divergence combined with evidence-based absorption can mitigate persona-environment self-locking in AI agents.

item.title: Researchers distill an 8B reasoning model into a 0.6B on-device student for structured text enrichment, achieving faster processing and partial quality recovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers distilled an 8-billion-parameter reasoning teacher model into a 0.6-billion-parameter student model for on-device structured text enrichment, mapping news articles to JSON objects with summaries and labels. The student runs significantly faster, processing articles in about 0.8 seconds compared to the teacher's 39 seconds, and recovers 58% of the quality gap in summaries, outperforming baseline methods like constrained decoding and few-shot prompting. The study included controls with a same-size non-reasoning teacher and a larger managed pipeline, evaluated by a blinded three-judge panel against full articles. The results show that the reasoning teacher transfers writing quality, while the managed pipeline improves label diversity, and a same-size instruction teacher helps students stay more grounded on short, thin-source articles. However, no single teacher model excelled in all aspects, leading to a proposed per-field routing map for on-device enrichment. The findings highlight trade-offs between reasoning capabilities, label diversity, and grounding in distillation for efficient on-device text processing.

item.title: Researchers propose INTENT, an LSTM-based framework predicting vehicle intentions at intersections with 99.71% accuracy on the InD dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The INTENT framework uses a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to predict vehicle intentions-going straight, turning left, or turning right-two seconds before the event at intersections. This prediction aims to improve autonomous vehicle safety and agility by enabling timely evasive actions in complex driving scenarios such as intersections, roundabouts, and emergency stops. The model was extensively tested with ablation studies on the InD dataset, achieving high accuracy of 99.71%. The study highlights the importance of incorporating human-like interpretation of driver intentions to enhance autonomous vehicle decision-making and trajectory prediction.

item.title: Researchers identify knowledge-circuit misalignment causing memorized facts in large language models to fail in downstream generalization tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied why fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) can memorize new facts but fail to apply them in reasoning tasks, defining this as the Knowing--Using Gap characterized by an accuracy gap and delay between memorization and generalization. They introduced a technique called self-patching to track how knowledge spreads internally and found that memorized information may not reach computation-effective layers due to knowledge-circuit misalignment. The team developed a heuristic that recovers 58-75% of the potential improvement in generalization, with experiments confirming the robustness of these findings across different domains.

item.title: Researchers use AI to identify and generate facial stimuli that highlight perceptual differences in emotion recognition between autistic and neurotypical adults [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed population-specific neural network models to predict facial emotion perception differences between autistic and neurotypical adults, finding that these differences are concentrated in a small subset of facial expressions. They used these models to select novel faces that maximize group separation and applied generative adversarial networks to transform images toward greater predicted group agreement. Validation showed that model-selected images amplified behavioral differences, while synthesized images reduced them, establishing a framework for optimized behavioral assays that reveal neurodivergent perceptual patterns beyond averaging across fixed stimulus sets.

item.title: Researchers develop patient simulator to evaluate health chatbots, finding communication style affects triage accuracy and highlighting risks of idealized AI interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed 2,053 real patient-chatbot conversations and found wide variation in communication patterns and emotional expression. They developed a patient simulator modeling clinical content, emotional state, conversational strategy, and communication style, which human graders found nearly indistinguishable from real conversations in a Turing-inspired test. Using five distinct patient personas across 1,164 clinician-graded cases, the team evaluated four large language models for urgency assessment and found that communication style significantly influenced triage outcomes. The study emphasizes that patient-centered conversational AI must accommodate diverse communication styles to avoid underperformance and potential amplification of health disparities in real-world deployments.

item.title: Researchers propose a proactive memory agent to address behavioral state decay in long-horizon tasks, improving decision-making in AI agents across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a proactive memory agent that operates alongside existing action agents to actively update a structured memory bank and selectively inject memory-grounded reminders, addressing the issue of behavioral state decay where relevant information is lost over long task trajectories. This approach is plug-and-play with current agents and demonstrated improvements of +8.3 and +6.8 percentage points in pass@1 accuracy on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and τ²-Bench, respectively. Ablation studies show that selective intervention outperforms other memory strategies such as passive exposure and always-on injection. The team also trained the Qwen3.5-27B model using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on the SETA dataset, achieving improved validation rewards and partial transfer to Terminal-Bench.

item.title: Researchers propose memory backtracking and topological attribution methods to explain Temporal Graph Networks, improving interpretability across nine temporal graph datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed new explanation methods for Temporal Graph Networks (TGNs) that incorporate the memory module, which records and updates node histories, to better understand which historical events influence model predictions. Their approach uses a topology attribution tree to capture neighbor influences and a memory backtracking tree to quantify how past events shape node memory vectors, applying Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to ensure event contributions match model logits. The method addresses limitations of existing explanations by optimizing event selection despite nonlinear mappings from logits to probabilities. Experiments on nine temporal graph datasets covering node property prediction, link prediction, and graph classification demonstrate that this approach provides more faithful explanations and outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further use and validation.

item.title: Researchers introduce Local Linear Transformer for PDE operator learning, combining linear global attention with local spatial mixing to improve accuracy and efficiency across various PDE problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed the Local Linear Transformer (LLT), a neural operator architecture designed to learn partial differential equation (PDE) solution maps more efficiently. LLT addresses limitations of standard transformer attention, which scales quadratically with computational nodes and lacks local interaction bias, by combining linear global attention with local spatial mixing and incorporating coordinate and geometry information. The team evaluated LLT on multiple PDE problems including elasticity, plasticity, airfoil flow, pipe flow, and Darcy flow, using data from finite-element, finite-volume, and finite-difference discretizations on both structured and unstructured meshes. LLT achieved competitive or lower relative L2 errors compared to existing neural operator and transformer baselines, while reducing training iteration time by factors of 1.8 to 2.5 on structured discretizations. The approach was also scaled to a 3D car aerodynamics dataset with over 32,000 unstructured mesh points per sample, demonstrating its accuracy and computational efficiency across diverse PDE settings.

item.title: ReCoLoRA introduces spectrum-aware recursive consolidation for continual fine-tuning of large language models, improving performance on multi-task GLUE benchmarks with fewer parameters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: ReCoLoRA (Recursive Consolidation of Low-Rank Adapters) is a new framework for continual fine-tuning of large language models that addresses the issue of task interference in LoRA-style methods by recursively decomposing and consolidating low-rank adapters. It initializes adapters using randomized SVD, selects per-layer ranks via an elbow criterion, and adapts the principal subspace before opening residual capacity, allowing each new task to build on previously learned representations. Evaluated on a six-task continual GLUE sequence across four 7-8 billion parameter backbones, ReCoLoRA outperforms several baseline methods on three backbones while training fewer parameters, with an oracle-routed task-bank variant providing an upper bound under full task isolation.

item.title: Omni-Sleep introduces a sleep foundation model using hierarchical contrastive learning of CNS and ANS dynamics, pre-trained on over 100,000 hours of multimodal polysomnography data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Omni-Sleep is a new sleep foundation model that incorporates the physiological organization of the central nervous system (CNS) and autonomic nervous system (ANS) by using their partition as a prior for topology-constrained representation learning. It learns structured representations through objectives that capture intra-system consistency, inter-system synchronization, and long-horizon sleep dynamics. The model was pre-trained on a large dataset of multimodal polysomnography signals including EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG, and respiration, and evaluated on sleep staging and multi-disease classification tasks. Omni-Sleep outperforms existing foundation-model baselines across datasets and modality-ablation settings, demonstrating improved label efficiency, generalization, and robustness to missing data. These results emphasize the importance of physiological hierarchy in developing generalizable sleep representation models. The code for Omni-Sleep is publicly available.

item.title: Researchers propose SHIFT, a transformer-based survival prediction model handling incomplete genomic data without imputation, validated across multiple cancer cohorts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce SHIFT (Survival prediction Handling Incomplete Features using Transformer), a survival prediction model designed to handle incomplete and heterogeneous genomic data without relying on test-time imputation. SHIFT uses masked self-attention and feature-availability masks to base predictions solely on observed inputs, improving robustness to missing data patterns across different sequencing panels. The model was evaluated on glioblastoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma datasets with external validation across multiple cohorts, including scenarios with severe cross-cohort panel mismatches. SHIFT demonstrated strong generalization and outperformed standard survival baselines and imputation-based methods while using a single model for varying feature sets. Incorporating patients from incomplete cohorts during training also improved external performance, suggesting that partially observed data can be effectively utilized in multi-center survival prediction for precision oncology.

item.title: Researchers present a multi-agent framework coordinating diverse foundation models for improved cooperative reasoning and decision-making across scientific domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A new multi-agent framework coordinates multiple foundation models through independent drafting, structured critique, and consensus aggregation to enhance AI reasoning reliability. The system includes a scoring module evaluating semantic, numerical, and procedural aspects across agents. Ablation studies across various scientific benchmarks reveal that model heterogeneity, rather than framework structure or redundant sampling, drives significant performance gains, improving step-wise accuracy and reasoning quality. The heterogeneous configuration achieves a 2.3x improvement over homogeneous setups with reduced variance across difficulty levels, highlighting the importance of diverse specialized models for complementary error detection and reasoning refinement. The study discusses architectural principles and evaluation methods, emphasizing how heterogeneous multi-agent coordination supports transparent, auditable, and high-confidence AI decision-making in scientific and industrial applications.

item.title: Jet-Long introduces dynamic bifocal RoPE for efficient zero-shot long-context extension in LLMs, improving accuracy and throughput up to 128K tokens without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Jet-Long is a tuning-free method designed to extend the context length of large language models (LLMs) beyond their pretraining window by dynamically adjusting the rescaling factor of RoPE attention. It combines a local RoPE-faithful window with a long-range window that adapts to sequence length, preserving short-context fidelity while enabling clean extrapolation to long contexts. This approach incurs minimal inference overhead and achieves up to 1.39× throughput on Nvidia H100 GPUs. Evaluated on Qwen3 models with up to 128K token contexts, Jet-Long outperforms the RULER baseline by several percentage points and achieves the best accuracy on the HELMET-RAG benchmark, as well as the lowest perplexity on PG-19. The method also generalizes to hybrid attention architectures like Jet-Nemotron without retraining and maintains robustness to hyperparameter changes, facilitating practical deployment in long-context applications such as retrieval-augmented generation and agentic workflows.

item.title: MetaNCA framework learns local rules to self-organize neural network weights, generating diverse architectures without backpropagation and scaling to 2 million parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Meta Neural Cellular Automata (MetaNCA), a system that learns local update rules to iteratively adjust weights of artificial neural networks using only local interactions. The approach employs a novel Weight Transformer architecture with linear attention to aggregate signals from neighboring weights and hidden states, enabling the generation of feedforward MLPs, CNNs, and ResNets trained on MNIST and CIFAR-100 datasets. MetaNCA demonstrates the ability to generalize to unseen architectures and benefits from architectural diversity during training, offering a scalable alternative to traditional backpropagation methods for network weight generation.

item.title: Researchers model seven psychological disorder-like phenotypes in reinforcement learning agents using dose-controllable cognitive appraisal signals, revealing a two-dimensional affective space and treatment simulations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a framework to model seven psychological disorders-anxiety, mania, obsessive-compulsive checking, depression, impulsivity, addiction, and post-traumatic stress-in reinforcement learning agents by manipulating cognitive appraisal signals as adjustable parameters. This approach produced graded, monotone dose-response behaviors across over a thousand runs, with disorders organizing into a two-dimensional affective space and showing distinct recovery patterns under different interventions. The study found that removing certain disorder parameters reversed reward distortion disorders but not avoidance disorders, which improved under a graded exposure curriculum. Interactions between disorder parameters predicted comorbidity patterns. The framework also demonstrated transferability of three disorder models to a different 3D pixel environment with a standard convolutional agent, indicating its applicability beyond specific agent architectures or environments.

item.title: Researchers analyze deep reinforcement learning evaluation and design paradigms, revealing scaling laws and challenging established performance conclusions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper examines the foundational evaluation and design methods in deep reinforcement learning, focusing on the role of scaling laws and the relationship between algorithm performance and data regimes. The authors conduct extensive experiments showing that some prior research conclusions under canonical paradigms may be incorrect. Their work provides a detailed analysis of scaling, capacity, and complexity in deep reinforcement learning, contributing to a better understanding of its theoretical and practical aspects.

item.title: Researchers propose graph-regularized deep learning framework for EEG-based emotion recognition using psychologically grounded label structures, improving accuracy and reducing misclassifications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a graph-regularized deep learning framework for EEG-based emotion recognition that models emotions as interconnected nodes based on psychological theories, addressing limitations of treating emotion classes as isolated labels. The framework incorporates three regularization strategies-Graph Label Smoothing, Commuting distance via Graph Laplacian, and Sliced Wasserstein Distance-to penalize predictions that deviate from established emotion relationships. The approach was tested on three backbone architectures-AudioTransformer, Conformer, and DCGNN-and evaluated using SEED-IV and SEED-V datasets, showing up to a 5.42% increase in accuracy and a 39% reduction in psychologically implausible misclassifications. This method aims to enhance the performance ceiling of standard EEG emotion recognition models, with code planned for release.

item.title: Researchers review limitations of Large Language Model-driven theorem provers in formal mathematics and propose shift to AI research agents for frontier mathematical challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Recent advances in AI for Mathematics, particularly Large Language Model-driven theorem provers, have succeeded in generating formal proofs for well-defined problems using Interactive Theorem Proving languages. However, these systems struggle with frontier research mathematics tasks like discovering new theorems or resolving open conjectures, which are often open-ended and abstract. The authors argue for a shift from predefined problem solvers to AI research agents capable of rigorous formal reasoning to tackle these challenges. The paper systematically reviews the field, covering datasets, auto-formalization, and proof synthesis, and identifies core limitations in current systems related to datasets, relational structures, mathematical exploration, tool ecosystems, and human-AI collaboration. It outlines a strategic roadmap for advancing AI in formal mathematical research.

item.title: Researchers present Shift & Drift, a zero-shot benchmark evaluating autonomous driving motion planners' generalization and robustness across semantic and state-distribution shifts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Shift & Drift, a dual-track benchmark designed to rigorously test autonomous driving motion planners on their ability to generalize to new urban environments and maintain robustness against execution perturbations. The benchmark includes a Semantic Shift Track that evaluates planners trained on North American and Singaporean data against scenarios from German cities and San Francisco, and a State-Distribution Drift Track that injects stochastic perturbations into vehicle dynamics to assess resilience to compounding errors. The study systematically evaluates various planning methods, finding that imitation learning approaches perform well on in-distribution data but struggle under semantic shifts and actuation noise, especially in pedestrian-dense settings. In contrast, reinforcement learning-based planners show more graceful degradation, maintaining higher safety and progress metrics. These results highlight a trade-off between imitation fidelity and closed-loop resilience, offering the community a rigorous tool to measure progress toward reliable autonomous driving deployment.

item.title: Barenholtz's autogenerative theory enriches Harrisean Integrationism by addressing structural gaps in language's prospective openness and semiotic continuity, with implications for LLM design [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Roy Harris's Integrationist linguistics critiques traditional computational language models by framing language as a situated, bipartite activity aimed at joint action rather than a fixed code. However, it leaves gaps in explaining how signs maintain openness, the link between linguistic and non-linguistic signs, and the structure of accumulated past interactions. This paper argues that Elan Barenholtz's autogenerative theory, developed in response to Large Language Models (LLMs), fills these gaps without contradicting Integrationism's core principles. The autogenerative theory offers a structural mechanism for the openness central to bipartite communication, a computational correlate for the continuity between language and other sign-making activities, and a theory of the archive representing past integrations. This synthesis preserves the primacy of situated integrative acts while providing explanatory content missing from Integrationism. For natural language processing researchers and LLM designers, the work clarifies what statistical structures LLMs exploit and their inherent limitations.

item.title: path_boost: A Python Package for Interpretable Graph-Level Prediction using Path-Based Gradient Boosting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.07935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present path_boost, a Python package for interpretable supervised learning on graph-structured input data. The package implements PathBoost, a gradient boosting algorithm that automatically discovers predictive labeled paths within graphs during the learning process. Unlike graph neural networks, which are generally difficult to interpret, PathBoost produces an additive prediction model over path-based features that explicitly reveals which substructures drive predictions. To avoid an exhaustive enumeration of all possible paths, the algorithm iteratively selects and extends paths during learning based on their predictive power, using boosting to combine weak learners into a strong ensemble. The package supports both regression and binary classification. Key features include compatibility with scikit-learn workflows, support for custom base learners and selectors, automatic starting node selection, parallel training across anchor nodes, and built-in variable importance computation. We demonstrate PathBoost on molecular property prediction of transition metal compounds, where atoms serve as nodes and bonds as edges, and further benchmark PathBoost against an established graph neural network and a graph kernel method across six molecular datasets. The package is available on PyPI and GitHub under an open-source license.

item.title: Linear Attention Architectures: Mechanisms, Trade-offs, and Cross-Layer Routing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.07953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-attention lets each token retrieve information from the full context, but its quadratic cost in sequence length limits training and inference at long context. This paper presents a comparative study of softmax attention and four recent recurrent linear-attention architectures: DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, and Gated DeltaNet-2. We express these mechanisms in a common recurrent-memory notation, making explicit how they differ in expressivity, memory decay, erase and write control, training throughput, and implementation complexity. Our experiments center on 350M-parameter models trained for 15B tokens, and include optimizer and learning-rate comparisons, hybrid-versus-pure stack comparisons, sequence-length runtime measurements, larger DeltaNet runs at 1.3B and 3B parameters, and a small set of downstream evaluations. The reported speed results measure training throughput and iteration time; we do not provide an empirical inference-speed benchmark. Within the reported 350M-parameter, 15B-token sweep, Kimi Delta Attention with Muon reaches the lowest final validation loss, a pure Gated DeltaNet stack trained with AdamW has the highest normalized training throughput, hybrid stacks generally improve loss at a throughput cost, and Muon consistently lowers final validation loss relative to AdamW in the matched architecture settings we evaluate. We introduce and evaluate lightweight cross-layer routing mechanisms for DeltaNet-style memories. The most natural DeltaNet-inspired formulation, forwarding a lower layer's delta-rule write error into the next layer's value target, does not improve over matched baselines. Routing into the aligned hidden stream and forwarding the write value instead yields a modest improvement in the matched runs we report: Cross-Layer Value Routing (CLVR) lowers final validation loss for both DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet.

item.title: A Multi-cluster Boundary Learning Method for Out-of-Scope Intent Detection via MiniLM Embedding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.07974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intent detection is a critical task that bridges human intents and system actions in human-machine interaction systems. However, there still exist challenges for detecting out-of-scope (OOS) intents. (i) The traditional methods view the OOS intent detection as a multi-class classification, then the detection accuracy decreases as the class number of the known intents increases; (ii) LLM-embedding methods require large parameters, that makes them difficult to train and practically deploy. Thus, this work proposes a multi-cluster boundary learning method to detect OOS intents via MiniLM embedding (i.e., all-MiniLM-L6-v2) in an one-class classification workflow. The method learns the boundaries of multi-cluster embeddings generated by MiniLM from the training utterances, and then rejects the out-of-domain utterances as OOS intents. Experiments are conducted on public CLINC150, StackOverflow and Banking77 datasets. The results show that the method achieves the state-of-the-art OOS intent detection performance compared the other baselines. Ablation studies are also conducted and the results show that the used MiniLM can better adapt to the workflow and utterance embedding requirements. The code is available at supplementary materials.

item.title: A Reliability Assessment of LALM Audio Judges for Full-Duplex Voice Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.07985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the empirical reliability of Gemini models as audio judges that score full-duplex agent conversations directly from the raw stereo waveform, tested across three models in the Gemini family: 2.5 Flash, 3.5 Flash, and 3.1 Pro. Our primary evidence base uses Gemini 2.5 Flash as the ground-truth model, validated against three calibrated human raters on 209 stereo sessions, scored on 8 production dimensions: 152 full-duplex conversations across 13 accent-and-condition strata, together with 57 adversarial defect-injected clips. The evidence for Gemini 2.5 Flash is consistent across three tests. (i) On 5 of 8 dimensions the LALM-human Spearman rho departs from the pairwise human-human rho by at most 0.07, and on 7 of 8 dimensions the two quantities 95 percent bootstrap confidence intervals overlap. (ii) The LALM agrees with the three-rater human mean within 1 point on 60 to 92 percent of sessions on 6 of 8 dimensions. (iii) On 45 of 48 (defect, dimension) cells the LALM is as sensitive as humans or better under Newcombe-Wilson 95 percent confidence intervals, though most of these are underpowered nulls rather than demonstrated parity. Rank-ordering ability transfers across the Gemini family: 3.5 Flash improves simple agreement to 8 of 8 dimensions, while 3.1 Pro rates several dimensions markedly lower than humans despite comparable rank correlation. A model swap should be re-validated on calibration specifically, not assumed from rank-correlation alone. We identify four areas where deployment requires care, and we estimate that human rating alone for our current evaluation cadence costs roughly two orders of magnitude more than the equivalent LALM workload. The data presented here provides a defensible empirical basis for deploying the LALM as a substitute or fourth rater on the dimensions where the evidence supports it.

item.title: Who Broke the System? Failure Localization in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.07989v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems enable complex problem solving through coordinated reasoning and action, but their distributed structure also introduces new challenges in diagnosing system-level failures. When an execution fails, identifying which agent is responsible and at what point the trajectory first becomes irreversibly misdirected is difficult due to long-horizon interactions and tightly coupled agent behaviors. In this paper, we study the problem of failure localization in LLM-based multi-agent systems and present AgentLocate, a framework that attributes failures to both a specific agent and the earliest decisive step. AgentLocate combines an LLM-based judging mechanism with multi-perspective verification by independent evaluators, whose assessments are aggregated using a confidence-aware strategy. The resulting feedback is further used to adapt the judge through lightweight fine-tuning, improving attribution quality. We evaluate AgentLocate on two complementary benchmarks covering diverse tasks, agent configurations, and trajectory lengths. Experimental results show that AgentLocate consistently outperforms existing failure localization methods in identifying both responsible agents and failure steps, while remaining efficient in terms of token usage and running time.

item.title: SpO$_2$ Predictor-Guided Stage-Wise Time-Frequency Reconstruction of Low-Quality Dual-Wavelength PPG for Oxygen Saturation Estimation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.07996v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Continuous oxygen saturation (SpO$_2$) estimation from wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) is important for long-term health monitoring, but low-quality red and infrared PPG segments can distort waveform morphology and degrade SpO$_2$ prediction accuracy. Existing PPG denoising and reconstruction methods usually optimize waveform fidelity or heart rate characteristics, while time-domain waveform loss on PPG signals alone insufficiently preserves frequency structure and SpO$_2$-relevant information. This paper proposes a SpO$_2$ predictor-guided stage-wise time-frequency reconstruction framework for low-quality dual-wavelength PPG signals. The proposed method first selects high-quality PPG segments to pretrain a SpO$_2$ predictor. A masked reconstruction model is then trained to recover randomly masked PPG regions using a joint reconstruction objective that combines time-domain waveform loss with frequency-domain loss computed from the short-time Fourier transform (STFT). To make the reconstruction task physiologically relevant, the pretrained SpO$_2$ predictor is incorporated as an additional constraint, encouraging the reconstructed PPG to preserve SpO$_2$ information rather than only minimizing waveform reconstruction error. The SpO$_2$ predictor and PPG reconstructor model are optimized through four training stages. Experiments on the public OpenOximetry Repository and a private wearable PPG dataset show that the proposed approach achieves the lowest subject-level MAE, with 2.882\% on the public dataset and 2.359\% on the private dataset.

item.title: Beware What You Autocomplete: Forensic Attribution of Backdoored Code Completions [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models have enabled powerful code completion systems that assist developers by predicting subsequent lines of code. However, these models remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious fine-tuning data covertly implants unsafe behaviors. Despite advances in defensive techniques, adaptive and sophisticated backdoor attacks still evade detection and mitigation. We present CodeTracer, a forensic framework that traces malicious code completions back to the backdoor fine-tuning data responsible for them. Operating under realistic post-deployment constraints, CodeTracer relies solely on the fine-tuning corpus and the reported miscompletion event. It extracts a structured behavioral fingerprint from the compromised output, narrows the search to semantically relevant code samples, and employs LLM-based reasoning to attribute unsafe logic to specific backdoor data. Extensive evaluations across three representative vulnerability cases and ten backdoor attacks, along with sixteen competitive baselines, demonstrate that CodeTracer consistently achieves high forensic accuracy, low false identification rates, and strong robustness against adaptive attacks.

item.title: Provably Optimal Learning Algorithms for Assistance Games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies an online variant of the assistance games framework, where an informed agent and an uninformed agent repeatedly interact over $T$ timesteps to optimize a common reward function. While the informed agent (the human) observes a latent state of the world, the uninformed agent (the assistant) observes only the human's actions. We provide the first provably efficient learning algorithms for repeated assistance games. We introduce the notion of assistance regret: the gap between the cumulative utility of interactions and that of the optimal joint policies in hindsight, which map latent states to action pairs. We present decentralized algorithms for both the human and the assistant that achieve a $(1-1/e)$-approximate assistance regret rate of $\widetilde{O}(T^{3/4})$, with runtime polynomial in the size of the action and state spaces. These algorithms are general; in particular, they accommodate any no-regret algorithm for the assistant. We prove that achieving a regret approximation factor better than $(1-1/e)$ is computationally intractable. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these generic no-regret algorithms can be tailored to a pseudo-decentralized setting -- using a shared random string -- to achieve a rate of $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/2})$, optimal up to logarithmic factors.

item.title: Can We Trust LLM's Logic? Quantifying Uncertainty, Coherence, and Robustness via a Graph-Based Framework [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-Language Models (LLMs) can be prone to flawed and unfaithful reasoning that decoding strategies like Self-Consistency (SC) fail to detect as they evaluate only final-answer agreement while ignoring the logical validity of intermediate steps. This raises three fundamental questions: How can we reliably quantify uncertainty in LLM reasoning? Can semantic, structural, and causal awareness select more faithful reasoning compared to na\"ive majority voting? and How robust is reasoning topology under adversarial conditions? To address these questions, we introduce GRAPHEVAL, a graph-based reasoning framework that re-frames uncertainty quantification (UQ) as a holistic reasoning fidelity problem. We propose a novel UQ metric, Graph Reasoning Coherence Score (GRCS), that quantifies semantic-structural consensus of the reasoning space and captures pathological mode collapse and confident hallucinations. We find that GRCS is the only metric that is consistently negatively correlated with reasoning faithfulness across both more capable and smaller models. Additionally, we introduce Graph Self-Consistency (GSC), a medoid-based decoding strategy that trades nominal accuracy for reasoning fidelity, exposing the degree to which SC is inflated by unfaithful lucky guesses in smaller models, while preserving or improving accuracy in more capable ones. Finally, through adversarial medoid ablation, we demonstrate that the GSC-selected path acts as a "load-bearing path" and forcing models away from it degrades reasoning faithfulness and, in targeted cases, causes drops in accuracy.

item.title: APIVOT: Adaptive Planning with Interleaved Vision-Language Thoughts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08024v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-horizon robot planning requires jointly reasoning over semantic task structure and geometric feasibility. To successfully execute a task, a robot must decompose goals, select task-relevant objects, and sequence actions, while ensuring that plans satisfy spatial constraints such as limited free space and object collisions. In this work, we propose APIVOT, a VLM-based planner that adaptively interleaves language and visual thoughts for long-horizon planning. APIVOT learns to leverage language for semantic reasoning, while using visual thoughts as imagined future states for internal verification of geometric feasibility. On long-horizon kitchen tasks, APIVOT outperforms general-purpose VLMs and prior planning frameworks, achieving the largest gains in spatially constrained settings. We find that APIVOT learns meaningful modality selection behavior, demonstrating that adaptive interleaving of vision-language thoughts improves both planning success and reasoning efficiency.

item.title: Structured Pruning of Large Language Models via Power Transformation and Sign-Preserving Score Aggregation with Adaptive Feature Retention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes an improved structured pruning method for large language models (LLMs) that addresses key challenges in adapting Adaptive Feature Retention (AFR), an unstructured pruning technique, to structured pruning. When applying AFR to structured pruning, three major problems arise: distribution mismatch between heterogeneous pruning scores, loss of sign information indicating optimization direction consistency, and influence of outliers. To address these issues, we propose a unified approach combining power transformation for nonlinear distribution alignment, sign-preserving score aggregation, and percentile-based outlier removal. Experiments on Llama-3-8B, Vicuna-v1.5-13B, and LLaVA-v1.5-13B demonstrate that our method maintains accuracy comparable to unstructured pruning while achieving practical inference speedup through structured pruning.

item.title: PLURAL: A Global Dataset for Value Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used worldwide, yet disproportionately reflect Western values, limiting their ability to represent diverse value systems. We introduce PLURAL, a large-scale, value-focused preference dataset grounded in the Integrated Values Survey (IVS), a nationally representative survey spanning 92 countries. Using a two-stage generation pipeline, we transform survey responses into synthetic preference triplets that preserve normative value signals while producing realistic scenarios. We release an initial version of PLURAL containing ~500,000 preference triplets representing people in 20 diverse countries. We evaluate PLURAL in three ways: (i) dataset-level validation showing that it preserves both cross-country value differences and within-country diversity from the original survey; (ii) automated evaluation showing that training on PLURAL improves alignment with target countries' cultural profiles, reducing mean absolute error by up to 27.7% relative to strong baselines; and (iii) blind human evaluation with 176 evaluators in India, Brazil, and Japan, who judge PLURAL-aligned responses as more representative of their national values. Together, these results show that PLURAL contains learnable signal for value steering, offering a scalable resource for pluralistic alignment. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/agdhruv/plural-alignment

item.title: What LLM Forecasters Know but Don't Say: Probing Internal Representations for Calibration and Faithfulness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models fine-tuned for forecasting can be accurate yet poorly calibrated, and their chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning may not faithfully reflect the evidence behind a forecast. We ask whether internal representations offer a more direct window into both. Working with Eternis-Forecaster 8B on OpenForesight, we train representation-pooling probes on intermediate activations and find they achieve substantially better calibration; a result that also holds for GLM-4.7-Flash and GLM-4.5-Air. We then assess CoT faithfulness through evidence ablation and diversionary injection: removing an influential source in the prompt often changes the model's forecast while leaving the reasoning trace untouched. The same probes function as lie detectors: their activations track behavioral shifts far better than the reasoning trace does, and they also predict the direction of change in 84% of cases, including when the CoT conceals the perturbation's influence. Finally, forced answering reveals that forecasts are largely fixed before reasoning begins: a single pre-reasoning pass recovers the committed answer and confidence, and routing questions by the spread of this pre-set answer distribution saves 30-47% of generated tokens, with no loss of accuracy. Together, these results establish probing internal representations as a practical tool for calibrating, auditing, and triaging language model forecasters and reasoning models more broadly.

item.title: Who Analyses the Analyser? Self-Validating LLM Hazard Analysis with Constitutional Meta-STPA [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted to draft the artifacts of safety analysis such as, losses, hazards, Unsafe Control Actions (UCAs), and safety constraints, inside rigorous processes such as Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA). Yet a blind spot runs through this fast-growing literature: every system gets analysed except the LLM-assisted tool doing the analysing, which is itself a safety-relevant system that can hallucinate standards, emit unverifiable constraints, and leave no audit trail from prompt to artifact. We take seriously the question the field has skipped -- {who analyses the analyser?} and answer it by turning STPA on the tool itself. We present \{Constitutional Meta-STPA}, an LLM-assisted STPA tool built around a closed loop: the tool runs a {meta-STPA} of the class of AI-assisted safety tools and {derives} rather than asserts, its governance constitution from the resulting loss$\to$hazard$\to$UCA$\to$constraint chain, yielding a published constitution of $21$ Tool Principles and $8$ Meta-Safety Principles, each bound to a code enforcement point. We formalise the measured object as a constitution-marginal coverage operator over a principle set $P$ ($|P|{=}29$) with a soundness lemma that isolates coverage from model and scanner, and report four findings. {(i)~Self-derivation:} a frontier ensemble ({claude-opus-4.8}${+}${claude-sonnet-4}) recovers $18/21$ canonical and all $8/8$ governance principles from the tool's own design, while a weaker pair recovers $12/21$ and $3/8$, so the meta layer is model-limited, not constitution-limited, and the same $8/8$ re-emerge from a second, independently authored tool.

item.title: Reinforcing the Generation Order of Multimodal Masked Diffusion Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently achieved substantial progress in natural language generation tasks. Recent research demonstrates that adaptive token generation ordering can significantly improve performance in mathematical reasoning and code synthesis applications. In this work, we investigate the optimization of generation order for both text-to-image synthesis and multimodal understanding. We first establish that, unlike structured problems in language generation such as Sudoku puzzles, model logits alone are insufficient for determining optimal generation sequences in text-to-image generation and multimodal understanding. To address this challenge, we introduce a learnable control module trained via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to determine the generation order. Our results demonstrate that learning this control block substantially improves both text-to-image alignment and multimodal understanding in DLMs. In particular, it enhances the model's ability to capture fine-grained spatial relationships in generated images while also strengthening performance on multimodal reasoning and comprehension tasks. We evaluate our framework on GenEval, an object-focused benchmark for text-to-image alignment, where it achieves 4.08% relative improvements. In addition, experiments on VLMEvalKit confirm 4.85% relative improvements in multimodal understanding, highlighting the broad effectiveness of our approach.

item.title: When Thinking Hurts: Epistemic Signals in the Reasoning Chains of Visual Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncertainty quantification for visual language models (VLMs) conventionally targets the answer token distribution. We provide the first three-family empirical characterisation of answer entropy behaviour in thinking-mode VLMs. Running four models on identical POPE adversarial samples, we find three qualitatively distinct patterns: Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking shows complete collapse (ans H AUROC = 0.492); GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking shows no collapse (0.716); and InternVL3-8B shows selective thinking (chains on only 50% of samples, ans H = 0.675 full / 0.602 thinking-only). Across all three thinking-mode models, thinking chain entropy outperforms answer entropy on the subset where chains are generated (0.647, 0.759, 0.608 vs. 0.492, 0.716, 0.602 respectively), suggesting chain signals are the more reliable predictor whenever chains are present. This holds strongly for Qwen and GLM, but with only marginal and statistically unreliable advantage for InternVL3 (n_FP = 17). A 300-sample VQAv2 pilot confirms chain entropy (0.680) outperforms answer entropy (0.595) on VQAv2 questions, with the gap largest for free-form answers (0.733 vs. 0.467). On harder reasoning tasks (HallusionBench) both Qwen models show moderate signal (approx. 0.64), consistent with incomplete pre-commitment on difficult questions. We additionally document structured abstention affecting 12-22% of queries with asymmetry toward absent-object queries, and a practical abstention gate raising accuracy from 71.0% to 93.8% at 62.7% coverage with no additional inference cost.

item.title: Deep Learning Method for Stationary Distribution of Reflected Brownian Motion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.08091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The stationary distribution of reflected Brownian motion (RBM) plays an important role in the analysis of high-dimensional stochastic systems, yet closed-form solutions are known only for a few special cases. Computing important performance metrics, such as tail probabilities, is even more intractable, despite their practical relevance. In this paper, we develop a deep learning approach that accurately and efficiently learns the Laplace transform of high-dimensional RBMs based on the basic adjoint relationship (BAR). Our framework combines a careful design of the loss function, training data sampling procedure, and neural network architecture. We evaluate the proposed method on RBM instances with known ground-truth tail probabilities and demonstrate near-perfect prediction in high-dimensional settings, highlighting its potential as a general tool for analyzing stochastic systems beyond analytically tractable regimes. Our code can be found at https://github.com/zhangz73/NN4MGF.

item.title: ICDAR 2026 HIPE-OCRepair Competition on LLM-Assisted OCR Post-Correction for Historical Documents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
